source: Ruis et al. (2023) The Goldilocks of Pragmatic Understanding: Fine-tuning strategy matters for implicature resolution by LLMs
finding: Binary implicature task (reply yes or no to an indirect answer). Base models, even large ones, stay near chance. Humans are far better.
numbers: Test set 600 items, each rated by 5 humans. Human mean 86.2%, best human 89.8%. Random about 50-55%. Best non-instruction-tuned class result: GPT-3-175B 5-shot 68.7%. All base models at least 17.5 points below the human mean.
limits: English only, one implicature format (yes/no). Humans err too. Sizes of API models are unknown.
agent_relevance: Size and raw pretraining do not give Gricean inference. The agent must not assume its first reading is the intended one.

source: Ruis et al. (2023) The Goldilocks of Pragmatic Understanding: Fine-tuning strategy matters for implicature resolution by LLMs
finding: Instruction tuning at the example level (not benchmark level) is what lifts implicature resolution. Benchmark-tuned models (T0, Flan) gain little from few-shot examples.
numbers: 0-shot to 5-shot: GPT-4 81.8% to 82.0%; ChatGPT 72.1% to 73.9%; text-davinci-003 71.2% to 79.7%; Cohere-command-52B 60.2% to 75.4% (+15.2); T0-11B 72.3% to 74.5%. GPT-4 5-shot is 3.9 points under the human mean.
limits: Cause is inferred from model families, not from a controlled ablation.
agent_relevance: Aligned chat models are the right base for pragmatic reading. Few-shot examples help weaker aligned models a lot, strong ones little.

source: Ruis et al. (2023) The Goldilocks of Pragmatic Understanding: Fine-tuning strategy matters for implicature resolution by LLMs
finding: Chain-of-thought helps implicature only for some models. For GPT-4 it reaches the human mean.
numbers: 5-shot to 5-shot CoT: GPT-4 82.0% to 86.5% (+4.5; human mean 86.2%); text-davinci-003 79.7% to 83.6% (+4.0); ChatGPT 73.9% to 77.2% (+3.3); text-davinci-001 74.5% to 67.3% (-7.2); Cohere-command 75.4% to 75.3% (-0.1). Item 'Is there a bus I can get to the station? You can't rely on it': GPT-4 5-shot wrong in 6 of 6 templates, with CoT right in 5 of 6.
limits: Six prompt templates, hand-written CoT. Sign of the gain depends on the model.
agent_relevance: Letting the model write out what the speaker meant before answering pays on strong models only. Gate it; do not force it on weak models.

source: Ruis et al. (2023) The Goldilocks of Pragmatic Understanding: Fine-tuning strategy matters for implicature resolution by LLMs
finding: Context-heavy (particularised) implicatures are harder than context-free (generalised) ones for both humans and models. Models fail on the same kinds of items humans find hard.
numbers: 217 of 600 test items hand-labelled: 47 generalised (e.g. 'You know all these people?' 'Some.' means No), 94 particularised (e.g. 'Want to stay for a nightcap?' 'I've gotta get up early.' means No). GPT-4 keeps a gap on particularised items even with few-shot; Cohere-command-52B matches GPT-4 on particularised but is lower on generalised.
limits: Small labelled subset; the other 383 items were left unlabelled as 'other'.
agent_relevance: Where the reply depends on the situation, put the situation in the prompt. S1 should carry speaker, goal and setting.

source: Ruis et al. (2023) The Goldilocks of Pragmatic Understanding: Fine-tuning strategy matters for implicature resolution by LLMs
finding: Scaling alone is slow for implicature. A linear fit says GPT-3-class models would need an impractical size to reach humans.
numbers: Gain from second-largest to largest model is 0.04% per billion parameters (GPT-3 6.7B to 175B) and 0.15% per billion (Cohere-command 6B to 52B).
limits: Extrapolation from two points per family.
agent_relevance: Do not wait for a bigger model to fix literal reading. Fix it in the scaffold.

source: Hu, Floyd, Jouravlev, Fedorenko, Gibson (2023) A fine-grained comparison of pragmatic language understanding in humans and language models
finding: Seven pragmatic phenomena, zero-shot multiple choice, same items given to humans. Largest models are above chance on all tasks and near human on some. They are weakest on humor, irony and maxims.
numbers: Human baseline 374 participants (Floyd et al., in prep). Smallest models (GPT-2, Flan-T5 base, InstructGPT ada 350M) at chance. Largest (Tk-Instruct 11B, Flan-T5 XL, text-davinci-002) above chance on all tasks except Tk-Instruct 11B on maxims. Accuracy jumps after 1B parameters. text-davinci-002 picks the human-preferred punchline 55% of the time.
limits: Old models (2022). Zero-shot, no CoT. Token-probability scoring of multiple choice.
agent_relevance: Tasks needing a broken or noticed social norm (irony, maxims) are the weak spot. Add a check: is the literal reading odd here?

source: Hu, Floyd, Jouravlev, Fedorenko, Gibson (2023) A fine-grained comparison of pragmatic language understanding in humans and language models
finding: Error patterns match humans. Among wrong answers, large models prefer the literal reading over lexical-overlap distractors, as humans do. So pragmatic failure is not a failure to get basic meaning.
numbers: Humans mostly pick Correct, sometimes Literal, rarely distractors. text-davinci-002 shows the same shape but picks Literal more often. Tk-Instruct 3B and Flan-T5 base prefer Literal; GPT-2 and ada at chance. In Metaphor, davinci-002 and Flan-T5 XL prefer the figurative distractor over the plain literal option.
limits: Qualitative comparison of answer distributions.
agent_relevance: The usual LLM miss is 'too literal'. Add a step asking what a cooperative speaker would intend.

source: Hu, Floyd, Jouravlev, Fedorenko, Gibson (2023) A fine-grained comparison of pragmatic language understanding in humans and language models
finding: Removing the context story hurts humans and models in the same order: irony most, then deceits, then maxims. Models stay good on word-scrambled text for most tasks except Metaphor, which hints at lexical shortcuts.
numbers: No-context human rerun: 30 participants. Models rerun: Tk-Instruct 11B, Flan-T5 XL, text-davinci-002. Scrambling: reasonable accuracy kept on all tasks but Metaphor.
limits: Human scrambling data not collected; authors expect humans would drop.
agent_relevance: A scramble probe is a cheap check that an answer used real structure (fits G3).

source: Amouyal, Meltzer-Asscher, Berant (2025) When the LM misunderstood the human chuckled: Analyzing garden path effects in humans and language models
finding: Humans fail garden-path comprehension questions, as the good-enough account says. LLMs also fail, on the same kinds of items.
numbers: Humans: 95.4% on simple questions (min 92.4, max 98.7), 37.0% on garden-path (GP) questions. Significance: plausible vs implausible p = 4.11e-16; GP vs non-GP p = .019 (implausible set), 2.52e-13 (reflexive set), .065 (plausible set). Verb transitivity bias vs accuracy r = 0.19.
limits: Human N not captured in my read. GPT-4 plausibility ratings built the plausible pairs.
agent_relevance: A model can misparse even with the full sentence in view. A restatement step is a real check.

source: Amouyal, Meltzer-Asscher, Berant (2025) When the LM misunderstood the human chuckled: Analyzing garden path effects in humans and language models
finding: Best model gets only 78% on GP comprehension questions. Larger models and more pretraining tokens track human item difficulty better. Chain of thought did not help.
numbers: o1-preview 78% (highest), Gemma-27B 74%. CoT: no significant change. Few-shot, 8 prompt variants per model. Kendall tau with human item difficulty rises with size in every family; OLMo-7B improves with more pretraining tokens, OLMo-1B does not.
limits: Only one closed family (OpenAI) tested. Yes/no questions.
agent_relevance: CoT does not remove a lingering wrong parse. Use an independent re-read or paraphrase, not 'think harder'.

source: Amouyal, Meltzer-Asscher, Berant (2025) When the LM misunderstood the human chuckled: Analyzing garden path effects in humans and language models
finding: A second probe, paraphrase, gives the same story. GP sentences are harder to paraphrase for all models. Text-to-image generation mirrors it.
numbers: Non-GP paraphrase accuracy above 90% for almost all LLMs under all manipulations. Among GP sentences, implausible ones have the highest paraphrase accuracy (models resist generating odd content such as 'The man hunted the child').
limits: Paraphrase scoring rule not captured in detail.
agent_relevance: Ask for a paraphrase and compare it with the original meaning in code; the test does not use the answer.

source: Zhang, Gibson, Davis (2024) Can Language Models Be Tricked by Language Illusions? Easier with Syntax, Harder with Semantics
finding: Four LMs (BERT, RoBERTa, GPT-2, text-davinci-003) on three human illusions. The syntactic illusion (NPI) tricks them, even more than humans. Semantic illusions (depth-charge) trick them little. So they are literal where humans are good-enough.
numbers: Depth-charge: only RoBERTa and GPT-3 (surprisal) show an illusion effect. NPI illusion: LMs more easily tricked than humans (e.g. all four LMs with perplexity for 'didn't'). Comparative illusion: baseline acceptable/unacceptable contrast captured in 6 of 8 model-metric tests. Human-like result counts: RoBERTa 10, GPT-3 9, BERT 8.5, GPT-2 8.
limits: Perplexity and surprisal, no prompting. Older non-chat models. Tests were counted, no effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Shortcut risk for the agent differs from the human one. Test the agent's own failure type; do not borrow human error rates.

source: Liu et al. (2023) We're Afraid Language Models Aren't Modeling Ambiguity
finding: New benchmark AmbiEnt: 1,645 linguist-annotated sentence pairs with a label set for each reading. Models cannot write the disambiguating rewrite.
numbers: 35.2% of examples are ambiguous. Crowdworkers agree with annotations 89.7% of the time; true disambiguations judged plausible 96.7%. Best model GPT-4: EDIT-F1 18.0, human-judged correct 32.0% (50 examples, 3 workers each). Copy-the-sentence baseline scores 0.
limits: NLI-based setup. Small human-evaluated sample.
agent_relevance: Listing possible readings is a task models do badly. Do not trust a self-made reading list as complete.

source: Liu et al. (2023) We're Afraid Language Models Aren't Modeling Ambiguity
finding: Models are not consistent with themselves about ambiguity, and NLI models are weak at recognising it.
numbers: For 76% of pairs of readings (d1, d2) of one sentence, GPT-4 says the sentence may mean d1 and may mean d2, yet also says it can only mean d1 and can only mean d2. True/false recognition: GPT-4 63.0% (random 50%). Best fine-tuned NLI model predicts the exact label set in 43.6% of instances. FLAN-T5 picks the right continuation preference 81.0% (random 32.8%).
limits: Template effects.
agent_relevance: Self-contradiction means a single-model self-check is unreliable (G4). Compare readings by code.

source: Liu et al. (2023) We're Afraid Language Models Aren't Modeling Ambiguity
finding: Use case: ambiguity detection can flag claims that fact-checks left open.
numbers: Recall of ambiguous claims 88.8%, precision 12.4%.
limits: Low precision; many hits were real ambiguities the fact-check did not mention, per authors.
agent_relevance: A high-recall, low-precision ambiguity flag is fine as a trigger for a clarify step, not as a verdict.

source: Tamkin, Handa, Shrestha, Goodman (2022) Task ambiguity in humans and language models
finding: AmbiBench: six ambiguous sentence-classification tasks. Large models trained with human feedback match or beat humans at finding the intended task from examples; scale alone or feedback alone is not enough.
numbers: With informative instructions humans are near perfect (all but one task); text-davinci-003 and -002 are closest. With 0 to 20 examples text-davinci-002 beats human participants; humans are close to j1-jumbo and curie. All models fall under a Bayesian oracle. With uninformative instructions, about 50% for humans and many models; humans score 100% on negation.
limits: Toy sentence features. Authors warn against claiming superhuman performance (one human sample).
agent_relevance: When a task is underspecified, show examples. They resolve it better than a vague instruction.

source: Tamkin, Handa, Shrestha, Goodman (2022) Task ambiguity in humans and language models
finding: Fine-tuning on a few ambiguous in-context examples lets a plain model generalise to new ambiguous tasks, passing the human-feedback model.
numbers: Fine-tune davinci on 68 examples from each of four tasks (272 total); test on 240 examples from the two held-out tasks. Controls fine-tuned on unambiguous versions do not improve.
limits: Training, not a scaffold.
agent_relevance: Out of scope for a no-training agent. Shows that resolving underspecification is learnable.

source: Zhang and Choi (2023) Clarify When Necessary: Resolving Ambiguity Through Interaction with LMs
finding: Three-step framework: decide when to ask, what to ask, then answer. INTENT-SIM estimates the entropy over simulated user intents to decide when to ask.
numbers: Tested on QA, machine translation and NLI. With a 10% question budget, INTENT-SIM roughly doubles the gain over random selection. Likelihood baseline AUROC 0.547. At budgets 10/20/30%, likelihood gives 76.1/78.1/79.8 versus 77.3/79.5/81.5 for a better method in the same table.
limits: Oracle makes the clarifying questions and answers. Simulated users, not real ones.
agent_relevance: Ready doctrine for G1: ask only on a measured signal (spread of intents), never on a schedule.

source: Kobalczyk, Astorga, Liu, van der Schaar (2025) Active Task Disambiguation with LLMs
finding: Treat clarifying questions as Bayesian experimental design. Sample candidate solutions and pick the question that splits them most evenly (expected information gain).
numbers: 20 questions (15 animals, 5 run seeds, 25 evaluation seeds) and code generation: 48 non-trivial HumanEval tasks and 47 APPS tasks, 3 run and 3 evaluation seeds. Models GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3 8B and 70B. Zero-shot GPT-4o-mini 35% on APPS vs 70% on HumanEval. EIG questions give higher final code accuracy with fewer queries than implicit and tree-of-thought question asking.
limits: Simulated answerer. Exact point gains are in tables I did not copy.
agent_relevance: Pick the question by its effect on the answer set, in code. This fits G5.

source: Kobalczyk, Astorga, Liu, van der Schaar (2025) Active Task Disambiguation with LLMs
finding: Reasoning in solution space beats reasoning in question space.
numbers: EIG-uniform beats implicit and implicit-ToT question strategies 'by a significant margin' in 20 questions.
limits: Same as above.
agent_relevance: Sample answers first, then ask what separates them.

source: Qiu, Zhang, Tenenbaum, Kim, Levy (2025) On the Same Wavelength? Evaluating Pragmatic Reasoning in Language Models across Broad Concepts
finding: Wavelength game, listening side. Strong models reach near-human accuracy and high correlation with direct prompting. Their answers are less varied than human answers.
numbers: Human data: 40 participants per item. Models: Llama3, Gemma3, Qwen3, DeepSeek-V3 and closed models. Accuracy rises with size. CoT lowers error and lowers Wasserstein distance to the human distribution. RSA adds nothing on top of CoT for comprehension.
limits: Numbers are in figures. One game, English.
agent_relevance: LLM answers are overconfident and spiky. Matters where code normalises probabilities (G5).

source: Qiu, Zhang, Tenenbaum, Kim, Levy (2025) On the Same Wavelength? Evaluating Pragmatic Reasoning in Language Models across Broad Concepts
finding: Speaking side. Rational Speech Act (RSA) reranking beats both direct and CoT prompting, with LM and human listeners as judges.
numbers: Judges: Qwen3-32B, Llama3-70B, and 5 human guesses per problem. RSA consistently better than direct and CoT. More alternatives help. Human-written clues still beat LM clues when humans judge. CoT does not always help in production.
limits: Gains are in figures, not copied. LM judge self-preference was checked by the human run.
agent_relevance: Concrete S1 operator: score each candidate phrasing by how well a simulated listener recovers the intent, pick in code.

source: Qiu, Zhang, Tenenbaum, Kim, Levy (2025) On the Same Wavelength? Evaluating Pragmatic Reasoning in Language Models across Broad Concepts
finding: Why RSA does not help comprehension: chain of thought already does RSA-like reasoning, and the model is overconfident so RSA cannot reshape its output.
numbers: Varying the quality of alternatives changed comprehension performance little (Appendix D.3). Chains of thought often list alternatives unprompted.
limits: Qualitative reading of chains.
agent_relevance: Do not stack a pragmatic prompt on a CoT that already does it. Test first (G7).

source: Muhlenbernd (2026) Social Meaning in Large Language Models: Structure, Magnitude, and Pragmatic Prompting
finding: Three frontier LLMs (GPT, Claude, Gemini) reproduce the direction of human social inferences from numerical (im)precision but distort the size. Pragmatics-based prompts help only in combination.
numbers: Case study from Solt et al. (2025) Experiment 1: six scenarios, six social attributes. Direction scores DAS = ISS = 1.0 for all models. Speaker-knowledge-and-motives prompt most consistently cuts magnitude error. Alternatives-only prompt can worsen it: Gemini interaction deviation 1.572 to 2.470. Combined prompt is the only one that improved all calibration metrics for every model: Claude Spearman 0.946, CCC 0.804, RMSE 0.576; Gemini CDS 1.480 to 1.338; GPT best CDS 0.304, RMSE 0.547.
limits: One paradigm, three models, no scalar implicature. Prompts only approximate RSA.
agent_relevance: Test any pragmatic prompt on magnitude, not only on direction. Listener-modelling prompts are safer than 'consider alternatives' alone.

source: Cong and Rayz (CogSci) LLMs and good-enough processing
finding: Argues LLMs show good-enough processing like humans, tested with prompting, probability measurement and lexical disturbance.
numbers: not read; download returned an empty file
limits: Search snippet only. Verify before use.
agent_relevance: If true, shallow reading is a model property too. Needs checking.

source: Paape (2023) Depth-charge illusion in humans and transformers
finding: Humans fall for the depth-charge illusion; Transformers reanalyse less and look more literal.
numbers: not read
limits: Search snippet only.
agent_relevance: Consistent with Zhang et al. (c12). Secondary.

source: NLPSI 2025 adversarial multi-agent debate for scalar implicature
finding: A Semantic Agent and a Pragmatic Agent debate a scalar implicature in a courtroom setup.
numbers: not read
limits: Search snippet only. Same-model debate conflicts with G4.
agent_relevance: Pattern of two readings in conflict. Do not use without testing.

source: Stanford CS224N report on RSA reference games with GPT-3 prompting
finding: Few-shot CoT said to improve davinci models a lot in an RSA reference game.
numbers: not read
limits: Student report, snippet only, low confidence.
agent_relevance: Weak support for CoT on reference games.
